food.text: At Kuk Swamp in the Wahgi Valley of Papua New Guinea, people began building agricultural drainage ditches around 9,000 years ago. They dug three major classes of ditches to turn the swampy lake basin into farmland, growing the native crop taro there.

Between about 6,900 and 6,400 years ago, the people of Kuk Swamp began growing bananas and sugar cane alongside their taro. This makes Kuk Swamp one of the earliest known sites in the world for the development of agriculture.

At Kuk Swamp in the New Guinea highlands, traces of taro exploitation have been dated to between 8250 BC and 7960 BC, among the earliest signs of people using this staple root anywhere in the world. It is still unclear whether this taro was deliberately cultivated or simply gathered from the wild.

Agriculture arose independently in the New Guinea highlands around 7000 BC, making this one of only a few places in the world where farming was invented from scratch rather than learned from elsewhere. This shift is best documented at Kuk Swamp, where farmers reshaped the wetland landscape over thousands of years.

Long before formal farming began, people in New Guinea were already eating wild taro and had domesticated other plants, including sago, the nut-bearing Canarium indicum, and the pandanus relative karuka. Canarium indicum may have been carried from the mainland out to the islands by early travelers.

By about 10,000 years ago, people at Kuk Swamp had gone beyond simple foraging, leaving evidence of cultivated plots and formalized agriculture already underway. Which exact plant they were growing at this early stage remains unknown.

Around 9,000 years ago, farmers at Kuk Swamp began digging drainage ditches to turn the wetland into cultivable ground, growing the native crop taro at the very edge of where it could survive in the highlands. Over time this reshaped the area into an anthropogenic grassland suited to farming.

Between about 6,900 and 6,400 years ago, farmers at Kuk Swamp expanded their fields beyond taro to include bananas and sugar cane. Archaeologists confirmed the bananas by finding tiny silica structures called phytoliths preserved in the ancient planting plots.

Researchers found unusually large numbers of banana phytoliths, tiny silica particles, in Kuk Swamp's ancient cultivation plots. Because bananas produce far fewer phytoliths than grasses, their abundance there between 6,950 and 6,550 years ago convinced researchers people were deliberately planting bananas rather than gathering wild ones.

The irrigation system at Kuk Swamp fell into three types of ditches: major disposal channels that diverted water away from the site, and larger and smaller field ditches that bordered the planting areas and connected back to those channels. Together they let farmers control water across their taro plots.

At Kuk Swamp, banana phytoliths turned up in far greater numbers than wild bananas normally produce, convincing researchers that the plants found between 6,950 and 6,550 years ago had been deliberately planted. These were Eumusa bananas, the group that became the largest and most significant line of domesticated bananas.

The bananas cultivated at ancient Kuk Swamp belonged to the Eumusa group, which went on to become the largest and most significant group of banana domesticates anywhere. Their cultivation there, alongside sugar cane, began between 6,900 and 6,400 years ago.

Before agriculture became established, people in New Guinea also began occasionally rearing cassowary chicks taken from the wild. This early step in managing a wild bird for food shows that pre-agricultural life involved more than simply gathering plants.
